claims.claim: Methuselah is the oldest confirmed living tree on Earth
claims.definition: Oldest CONFIRMED LIVING, NON-CLONAL tree (a single individual verified by dendrochronological ring count). Excludes clonal colonies (e.g. Pando) and unverified or model-based age estimates.
claims.current_record_holder: Methuselah (Pinus longaeva), White Mountains, California - exact location undisclosed by the U.S. Forest Service
claims.authoritative_source: Guinness World Records; USDA Forest Service
claims.notes: Two contenders could displace it: an unnamed bristlecone crossdated to 5,074 years in 2009 (core collected 1957; liveness not re-confirmed) and Gran Abuelo (alerce, Chile) claimed ~5,484 years in 2022 (model-based, not yet accepted). Proto3 as rendered said 'the oldest living tree on Earth' without the confirmation qualifier - corrected to 'oldest confirmed living tree'.

claims.claim: The tree is about 4,850 years old
claims.definition: Age by dendrochronological ring count of the living individual
claims.authoritative_source: Guinness World Records; USDA Forest Service

claims.definition: Crossdated germination estimate derived from core ring counts anchored to a continuous tree-ring chronology
claims.authoritative_source: Schulman 1958 / Harlan crossdating, cited by Guinness World Records and the U.S. Forest Service

claims.claim: Methuselah was already about 270 years old when the Great Pyramid was built
claims.definition: Computed: germination 2832 BC minus Great Pyramid completion ~2560 BC gives ~272 years, rounded to 270
claims.authoritative_source: Computed from methuselah_germination plus Great Pyramid dating (~2560 BC, academic consensus)

claims.claim: In 1964 a bristlecone pine (WPN-114, 'Prometheus') was cut down under a research permit and ring-counted at ~4,862-4,867 years - the oldest tree THEN KNOWN
claims.definition: Oldest known at the time of felling (1964) - NOT 'the oldest tree ever found', which is no longer true today
claims.current_record_holder: n/a (tree destroyed); today's confirmed oldest living is Methuselah
claims.authoritative_source: Donald R. Curry 1964 felling, Snake Valley, Nevada; Tom Harlan re-count - documented in the Rocky Mountain Tree-Ring Research database
claims.notes: Proto3 narration said 'The oldest tree ever found, destroyed in minutes.' This is no longer strictly true: the Harlan tree crossdated to 5,074 years (announced 2009, core collected 1957) exceeds Prometheus, and Gran Abuelo's ~5,484-year model estimate exceeds it further. Corrected to 'The oldest tree then known'.

claims.definition: The U.S. Forest Service deliberately does not disclose the tree's exact location to protect it from damage
claims.authoritative_source: USDA Forest Service / Inyo National Forest

claims.claim: Most of the tree is already dead - one thin strip of living bark keeps it alive
claims.definition: Strip-bark growth in ancient bristlecone pines: living cambium persists only along a narrow vertical strip; the rest of the trunk is dead wood. The scanner flags 'most' (a quantifier, not a record) - recorded here as a verified biology claim per V4 discipline.
claims.measured_value: qualitative - strip-bark form documented by the U.S. Forest Service and dendrochronology literature
claims.authoritative_source: USDA Forest Service - Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest, Inyo National Forest
